text: The gradient handles a function that turns many inputs into one number. A layer of a neural network, however, turns a vector into another vector, and to differentiate it we need a richer object, called the Jacobian matrix.

Recall the picture from module one: a matrix moves every point of the plane, and the grid lines stay straight and evenly spaced. A general function from two inputs to two outputs is less polite. It bends the grid, curving its lines in different ways in different places.

Yet zoom in on one small patch, and the curved grid looks straight again, just as a curve looked straight under the microscope when we met the derivative. Close up, the function behaves like a linear transformation, and the matrix of that local transformation is the Jacobian.

Its entries are partial derivatives arranged in a grid. Each row belongs to one output and each column to one input, so the entry in row i and column j says how much output i moves when input j is nudged. The first column shows where a small step along x lands, and the second column where a step along y lands, exactly like the columns of a matrix in lesson one point three.

Take the map that turns polar coordinates, a distance r and an angle theta, into ordinary x and y. Its Jacobian has determinant r, so a small patch far from the centre is stretched more than a patch close to it. That is the familiar fact that a ring further out covers more area, and it is the determinant from module one, now measured locally.

The chain rule now becomes matrix multiplication. Compose two functions and their local linear maps compose too, so the Jacobian of the whole is the product of the Jacobians, just as composing transformations multiplied their matrices. For a linear layer, y equals W times x, the Jacobian is simply the weight matrix W.

Backpropagation through a network multiplies a long chain of Jacobians, but it never builds them in full. Instead it carries one vector backwards and multiplies it by one Jacobian at a time, which is far cheaper. In a language model, every layer hands such a vector back to the layer before it during training. Next, linear approximation and Taylor series, which ask how far the zoomed in picture can be pushed.
